bones.name: l1
bones.function: The first lumbar vertebra, uppermost of the largest segments of the movable part of the vertebral column. Like all lumbar vertebrae it is distinguished by the absence of a foramen in the transverse process and the absence of costal facets on the sides of the body; its large body, wider from side to side than from before backward, carries the load of the trunk down toward the pelvis.
bones.note: The rib count may be increased by the development of a cervical or lumbar rib: Gray records that the transverse process of the first lumbar is sometimes developed as a separate piece, forming a lumbar rib — a peculiarity rarely met with.
bones.source: grays1918:are the largest segments of the movable part of the vertebral column

bones.name: l2
bones.function: The second lumbar vertebra, one of the largest segments of the movable part of the vertebral column. It shows the standard lumbar pattern — a massive body, no transverse-process foramen, and no costal facets — and transmits trunk load from L1 to L3 through its body and paired articular processes.
bones.source: grays1918:are the largest segments of the movable part of the vertebral column

bones.name: l3
bones.function: The third lumbar vertebra, the middle of the five largest movable segments of the vertebral column. Its large body, flattened or slightly concave above and below, bears trunk load between L2 and L4, and its transverse processes give attachment to muscles of the loin.
bones.note: Lumbar transverse processes are homologous with the ribs — Gray notes they are situated in front of the articular processes, instead of behind them as in the thoracic vertebrae.
bones.source: grays1918:are the largest segments of the movable part of the vertebral column

bones.name: l4
bones.function: The fourth lumbar vertebra, one of the largest segments of the movable part of the vertebral column, carrying load between L3 and L5. Like its neighbours it lacks a transverse-process foramen and costal facets, and its body, like its neighbours', is large, wider from side to side than from before backward, and a little thicker in front than behind.
bones.source: grays1918:are the largest segments of the movable part of the vertebral column

bones.name: l5
bones.function: The fifth and lowest lumbar vertebra, characterized by its body being much deeper in front than behind, which accords with the prominence of the sacrovertebral articulation. It is further marked by a smaller spinous process, a wide interval between the inferior articular processes, and thick transverse processes that spring from the body as well as from the pedicles.
bones.note: Its wedge-shaped body creates the prominent sacrovertebral angle where the mobile spine hands its load to the fixed sacrum.
bones.source: grays1918:characterized by its body being much deeper in front than behind

bones.name: t11
bones.function: An atypical lower thoracic vertebra whose body approaches in its form and size that of the lumbar vertebrae. The articular facets for the heads of the ribs are of large size and placed chiefly on the pedicles, which are thicker and stronger here than elsewhere in the thoracic region; the spinous process is short and nearly horizontal, and the very short transverse processes carry no articular facets, so rib 11 meets it only at its head.
bones.note: Because its transverse processes have no facets for rib tubercles, the eleventh rib articulates with the column by its head alone — one reason the last two ribs float.
bones.source: grays1918:the body approaches in its form and size to that of the lumbar vertebrae

bones.name: t12
bones.function: The last thoracic vertebra, with the same general characteristics as the eleventh, but distinguished by inferior articular surfaces that are convex and directed lateralward like those of the lumbar vertebrae. In the general form of its body, laminae, and spinous process it resembles a lumbar vertebra, making it the true transition bone between the rib-bearing and lumbar spine.
bones.note: Each transverse process is subdivided into three elevations — superior, inferior, and lateral tubercles — the superior and inferior corresponding to the mammillary and accessory processes of the lumbar vertebrae.
bones.source: grays1918:has the same general characteristics as the eleventh

bones.name: sacrum_bone
bones.function: A large, triangular bone formed of five fused vertebrae, situated in the lower part of the vertebral column at the upper and back part of the pelvic cavity, where it is inserted like a wedge between the two hip bones. Its base articulates with the last lumbar vertebra and its apex with the coccyx, so every load carried by the spine passes through it into the pelvis.
bones.note: Gray counts its articulations plainly: the sacrum articulates with four bones — the last lumbar vertebra above, the coccyx below, and the hip bone on either side. In the female it is shorter and wider than in the male, enlarging the pelvic cavity.
bones.source: grays1918:inserted like a wedge between the two hip bones

bones.name: coccyx
bones.function: The terminal bone of the vertebral column, usually formed of four rudimentary vertebrae (the number may be increased to five or diminished to three), all destitute of pedicles, laminae, and spinous processes. Its base presents an oval surface for articulation with the sacrum, its coccygeal cornua project upward to meet the cornua of the sacrum, and its apex gives attachment to the tendon of the external anal sphincter.
bones.note: The first coccygeal segment is the largest and often exists as a separate piece; at a late period of life, especially in females, the coccyx often fuses to the sacrum.
bones.source: grays1918:is usually formed of four rudimentary vertebrae

bones.name: sternum
bones.function: An elongated, flattened bone forming the middle portion of the anterior wall of the thorax, built of three pieces — manubrium, body, and xiphoid process. Its upper end supports the clavicles, and its margins articulate with the cartilages of the first seven pairs of ribs.
bones.note: At the junction of manubrium and body — the sternal angle (angulus Ludovici) — a facet on each piece combines to form the notch that receives the costal cartilage of the second rib; at the junction of the third and fourth pieces of the body a sternal foramen is occasionally seen.
bones.source: grays1918:elongated flattened bone forming the middle portion

bones.name: l_costal_cartilage
bones.function: The left set of costal cartilages: bars of hyaline cartilage which serve to prolong the ribs forward and contribute very materially to the elasticity of the walls of the thorax. The first seven pairs are connected with the sternum, the next three each articulate with the lower border of the cartilage of the preceding rib, and the last two have pointed extremities that end free in the wall of the abdomen.
bones.note: The cartilages increase in length from the first to the seventh, then gradually decrease to the twelfth; in old age they are prone to undergo superficial ossification.
bones.source: grays1918:bars of hyaline cartilage which serve to prolong the ribs forward

bones.name: r_costal_cartilage
bones.function: The right set of costal cartilages: bars of hyaline cartilage which serve to prolong the ribs forward and contribute very materially to the elasticity of the walls of the thorax. The first seven pairs are connected with the sternum, the next three each articulate with the lower border of the cartilage of the preceding rib, and the last two have pointed extremities that end free in the wall of the abdomen.
bones.note: The inferior borders of the sixth to ninth cartilages carry heel-like projections with smooth facets that articulate with the cartilage below — the interchondral joints that stitch the costal margin together.
bones.source: grays1918:bars of hyaline cartilage which serve to prolong the ribs forward

bones.name: l_rib8
bones.function: The left eighth rib, the first of the false (vertebrochondral) ribs: its cartilage reaches not the sternum but the lower border of the seventh costal cartilage above. Its head carries two facets that articulate with the bodies of two adjacent thoracic vertebrae (T7 and T8), and its tubercle meets the transverse process of T8.
bones.note: Sometimes the eighth rib cartilage articulates directly with the sternum; Gray records that this condition occurs more frequently on the right side than the left.
bones.source: grays1918:Sometimes the eighth rib cartilage articulates with the sternum

bones.name: r_rib8
bones.function: The right eighth rib, the first of the false (vertebrochondral) ribs: its cartilage reaches not the sternum but the lower border of the seventh costal cartilage above. Its head carries two facets that articulate with the bodies of two adjacent thoracic vertebrae (T7 and T8), and its tubercle meets the transverse process of T8.
bones.note: Sometimes the eighth rib cartilage articulates directly with the sternum; Gray records that this condition occurs more frequently on the right side — this side — than the left.
bones.source: grays1918:Sometimes the eighth rib cartilage articulates with the sternum

bones.name: l_rib9
bones.function: The left ninth rib, a false (vertebrochondral) rib whose cartilage joins the cartilage of the eighth rib above rather than the sternum. Its head articulates by two facets with the bodies of T8 and T9, and its tubercle with the transverse process of T9.
bones.note: The ribs vary in their direction, and the obliquity reaches its maximum at the ninth rib, gradually decreasing from there to the twelfth.
bones.source: grays1918:the obliquity reaches its maximum at the ninth rib

bones.name: r_rib9
bones.function: The right ninth rib, a false (vertebrochondral) rib whose cartilage joins the cartilage of the eighth rib above rather than the sternum. Its head articulates by two facets with the bodies of T8 and T9, and its tubercle with the transverse process of T9.
bones.note: The ribs vary in their direction, and the obliquity reaches its maximum at the ninth rib, gradually decreasing from there to the twelfth.
bones.source: grays1918:the obliquity reaches its maximum at the ninth rib

bones.name: l_rib10
bones.function: The left tenth rib, the lowest rib whose cartilage still joins the costal margin: it is a false (vertebrochondral) rib attached to the cartilage of the ninth rib above. Unlike the typical ribs it has only a single articular facet on its head, meeting the body of T10 alone.
bones.note: Gray lists the first, second, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth as the peculiar ribs — the ones whose features depart from the common pattern of the series.
bones.source: grays1918:has only a single articular facet on its head

bones.name: r_rib10
bones.function: The right tenth rib, the lowest rib whose cartilage still joins the costal margin: it is a false (vertebrochondral) rib attached to the cartilage of the ninth rib above. Unlike the typical ribs it has only a single articular facet on its head, meeting the body of T10 alone.
bones.note: Gray lists the first, second, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth as the peculiar ribs — the ones whose features depart from the common pattern of the series.
bones.source: grays1918:has only a single articular facet on its head

bones.name: l_rib11
bones.function: The left eleventh rib, a floating (vertebral) rib: free at its anterior extremity, it has a single articular facet of rather large size on its head, no neck or tubercle, and a pointed anterior end tipped with cartilage that ends in the wall of the abdomen. It articulates with the vertebral column only, at the body of T11.
bones.note: The eleventh rib retains a slight angle and a shallow costal groove, both of which the twelfth has lost.
bones.source: grays1918:have each a single articular facet on the head

bones.name: r_rib11
bones.function: The right eleventh rib, a floating (vertebral) rib: free at its anterior extremity, it has a single articular facet of rather large size on its head, no neck or tubercle, and a pointed anterior end tipped with cartilage that ends in the wall of the abdomen. It articulates with the vertebral column only, at the body of T11.
bones.note: The eleventh and twelfth ribs are each ossified from only two centers, the centers for the tubercles being wanting.
bones.source: grays1918:have each a single articular facet on the head

bones.name: l_rib12
bones.function: The left twelfth rib, the last and lowest floating rib: much shorter than the eleventh, with its head inclined slightly downward, a single articular facet meeting the body of T12, and neither neck, tubercle, angle, nor costal groove. Its anterior end is free and pointed, tipped with cartilage that ends in the wall of the abdomen.
bones.note: Sometimes the twelfth rib is even shorter than the first — the shortest rib in the body.
bones.source: grays1918:much shorter than the eleventh and its head is inclined slightly downward

bones.name: r_rib12
bones.function: The right twelfth rib, the last and lowest floating rib: much shorter than the eleventh, with its head inclined slightly downward, a single articular facet meeting the body of T12, and neither neck, tubercle, angle, nor costal groove. Its anterior end is free and pointed, tipped with cartilage that ends in the wall of the abdomen.
bones.note: Sometimes the twelfth rib is even shorter than the first — the shortest rib in the body.
bones.source: grays1918:much shorter than the eleventh and its head is inclined slightly downward

bones.name: l_inferior_nasal_conchae
bones.function: The left inferior nasal concha extends horizontally along the lateral wall of the nasal cavity and consists of a lamina of spongy bone, curled upon itself like a scroll. Its lateral surface is concave and forms part of the inferior meatus, into which the nasolacrimal canal — completed by the lacrimal bone and this concha — opens to transmit the nasolacrimal duct.
bones.note: It articulates with four bones — ethmoid, maxilla, lacrimal, and palatine — the descending process of the lacrimal meeting its lacrimal process to assist in forming the canal for the nasolacrimal duct.
bones.source: grays1918:consists of a lamina of spongy bone curled upon itself like a scroll

bones.name: r_inferior_nasal_conchae
bones.function: The right inferior nasal concha extends horizontally along the lateral wall of the nasal cavity and consists of a lamina of spongy bone, curled upon itself like a scroll. Its lateral surface is concave and forms part of the inferior meatus, into which the nasolacrimal canal — completed by the lacrimal bone and this concha — opens to transmit the nasolacrimal duct.
bones.note: Unlike the superior and middle conchae, which are parts of the ethmoid, the inferior concha is a separate bone in its own right, ossified from a single center in the wall of the cartilaginous nasal capsule.
bones.source: grays1918:consists of a lamina of spongy bone curled upon itself like a scroll

bones.name: r_palatine
bones.function: An L-shaped bone situated at the back part of the nasal cavity between the maxilla and the pterygoid process of the sphenoid. It contributes to the walls of three cavities — the floor and lateral wall of the nose, the roof of the mouth, and the floor of the orbit — its horizontal plate completing the posterior part of the hard palate on the right.
bones.note: The palatine articulates with six bones: the sphenoid, ethmoid, maxilla, inferior nasal concha, vomer, and the opposite palatine across the median palatine suture.
bones.source: grays1918:situated at the back part of the nasal cavity between the maxilla and the pterygoid process
